These products work, not in the allopathic "pharma-medicine" way, but in a terrain-support, consciousness bolstering plant-teacher sort of way.

recABS9cTyYGHFXEG.Body: The Sonic Slider is the flagship tool behind Biofield Tuning itself, a weighted tuning fork hand-tuned to 93.96 Hz, the twelfth harmonic of the Schumann Resonance, Earth's own natural electromagnetic pulse. Its extended handle lets you glide it smoothly across the face, neck, and body, and practitioners and users regularly report support for relaxation, circulation, and nervous system regulation. It's the same fork Chance uses in his own sessions, and a great entry point if you want to bring this work into your own daily routine.

recEBEDXpPbvCxQw5.Body: Melissa Kupsch is the Australian homeopath behind RMDY Collective and RMDY Academy of Homeopathy, and one of the clearest voices I know for homeopathy as true energy medicine. Her remedies work on the resonance principle, like cures like, where a matching frequency from nature is shown to the body so the vital force can recognize the distortion and resolve it. When Melissa joined Kyle Denton and me on InnerVerse, we explored the premise that spirit precedes form, and homeopathy demonstrates that principle as plainly as anything I know. RMDY makes quality remedies and first aid kits accessible, prepared with real care for who makes the medicine and how.

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Creativity as a spiritual path", "body": "Chance explained that he started InnerVerse after listening to podcasts in his early twenties, when positive voices helped replace repetitive thought patterns and supported a mindfulness practice. He first wanted to platform artists and creators, and he argued that creativity is the spiritual path of the unique individual because it demands self-work to move past plateaus. He described building a container for his creative energy, starting with an Etsy shop, and staying consistent until it grew. He rejected the idea of talent and credited time, effort and care. The host asked about the catalyst for his awakening, and Chance pointed to psychedelic experiences and festival culture."}, {"title": "Outsiders, fear and fractured friendships", "body": "The host asked how changing views had affected relationships over the previous sixteen or seventeen months. Chance described himself as a lifelong outsider who never joined groups easily. He recalled a two minute wave of fear of death early in the pandemic and said years of meditation had taught him to recognize it. He said invitations from friends faded, that he blocks people who turn disrespectful online, and that his Telegram group became a valued community. He also said he prefers leading by example over lecturing, and both hosts agreed that preaching often hides a need for approval."}, {"title": "Lost history and orgone technology", "body": "Asked for the most interesting thing he was learning, Chance described research into the world's fairs and the Civil War era sanitary fairs, which he suggested were used to spread an official version of American history and cover an earlier civilization. He proposed that earlier architecture and organ pipes worked as acoustic and energetic technology. The host asked about the ugliness of modern buildings. Chance then discussed orgone devices, his friend Mitch placing them near cell towers across Arizona, and a view that field coherence, grounding and tuning forks matter more than any gadget."}, {"title": "Starting with crystals", "body": "The host asked how a beginner could build a real relationship with crystals. Chance recommended inexpensive selenite, noticing the sensation near the palms and head, and compared it to the feeling of making energy balls in qigong. He said color, chemical makeup and growth shape can hint at a stone's properties, and that no crystal will fix your life on its own. Intention and a lasting relationship matter most. Asked about the New Age crystal trade, he allowed that commerce can exploit people yet also lead newcomers toward chakras and emotional health."}, {"title": "Technocracy, free will and crypto", "body": "Asked where the world was heading, Chance described technocracy and transhumanism as outward versions of an inner struggle, citing Michael Ende's The Neverending Story on false wishes and empty vessels. He argued that free will is the basis of life and that consent is harvested through gradual media conditioning. On crypto, he called it video game money, compared profits to the stock market, and warned it could become a government coin. He suggested real wealth such as land, water and food, and pointed listeners to his What Is Money episode with Dylan Saccoccio."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: I joined Joel Rafidi and Yerasimos Stilianessis for their new show, Here For The Truth. In this episode we discuss the importance of self-awareness, using crystals for beginners our nefariously changing history and the dark side of crypto currency, and tons more.
